title: Brain Science of Emotions
keyIdea: Emotions start in the brain. The amygdala, part of the limbic system, spots possible danger in a split second and sets off fight, flight or freeze. The prefrontal cortex, behind your forehead, checks a moment later and can calm the alarm. A flood of stress hormones makes it hard to think and recall. In the teenage years the dopamine reward system is very responsive, while the prefrontal cortex keeps developing into the mid-twenties. Suppressing a feeling hides it but the stress stays inside; regulating it, for example by naming it or by cognitive reappraisal, helps it settle.

kid: Deep inside your brain are two small, almond-shaped parts called the amygdala. They belong to the limbic system, brain parts linked to feelings and memory. The amygdala is like a smoke alarm. It spots anything that might be a threat, very fast, before you have even thought. When it goes off, your body gets ready for fight, flight or freeze. Adrenaline makes your heart pound within seconds. Cortisol builds up more slowly, over about 20 minutes. Then the prefrontal cortex, just behind your forehead, catches up and checks the facts. If the snake is only a stick, it calms the alarm.

A little alarm can help you focus. A flood of stress hormones does the opposite. It makes the prefrontal cortex work badly, so it is hard to think, plan or remember. That is why your mind can go blank in a scary test, even though you learned the answers. The memory is still there. Once you are calm, it comes back.

Your brain is still building. In the teenage years, the reward system, which uses a chemical called dopamine, becomes extra lively. The prefrontal brake is still being wired, and it is not finished until the mid-twenties. So feelings and thrills can feel very strong.

You can steer feelings. Pushing a feeling down, or hiding it, is called suppression. The feeling stays and your body stays stressed. Regulating works better. Name the feeling: I feel embarrassed. Breathe out slowly. Or try cognitive reappraisal: think of another true way to see what happened. Maybe my friend just did not see me.
adult: This topic is for ages 11 to 12, the move to secondary school. It fits the PSHE key stage 3 work on health and wellbeing, the RSHE mental wellbeing goals in England, and the CASEL skills of self-awareness and self-management. Pupils learn a simple, true model of how the brain makes and calms emotion. Then they try ways to manage feelings that have good evidence behind them.

Key terms: limbic system, amygdala, prefrontal cortex, the fight, flight or freeze response, adrenaline, cortisol, dopamine and the reward system. For coping: emotion regulation, suppression, naming the feeling and cognitive reappraisal. The model draws on LeDoux on threat, Arnsten on stress and the prefrontal cortex, and Steinberg and Casey on the teen brain. The lab shows average trends, not rules for any one child. Gross found that hiding a feeling does not make it fade. It raises heart rate and stress, and it blurs memory of the moment. Rethinking what happened lowers the feeling without those costs. Putting a feeling into words also calms the amygdala.

Common mistakes to watch for. Some think the amygdala is a fear centre to switch off. In fact it is a fast detector that also flags good surprises. Some think more stress always helps. High stress blocks working memory and recall. Some call the teen brain broken. It is still growing, and it learns fast. And some mix up reappraisal with pretending. Saying everything is perfect, or that you do not care, is not reappraisal.

In the lab, learners send surprises to a brain and see the fast alarm and the slower check. They drag a stress slider until test facts drop out of memory. They compare the reward system and the brake from age 6 to 26. They sort coping moves into suppress or regulate, and they pick realistic new thoughts. Every drag has a button twin.

familyTip: Next time someone in the family has a big reaction, wait until everyone is calm, then name it together: Your amygdala fired the alarm. Ask what the prefrontal cortex would say now, and find one other realistic way to see what happened. Adults can model this out loud about their own day.

Ask: what else could this mean?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fire the amygdala alarm, slide stress hormones and age, sort suppress or regulate, and reappraise.

practice.prompt: Which part of the brain spots possible danger first?
practice.hint: Think of the alarm in the lab.
practice.explain: The amygdala, in the limbic system, detects possible threats in a split second. The prefrontal cortex checks a moment later.

practice.prompt: On a simple model, you recall {a} facts out of 10 when calm and focused. Panic blocks {b} of them. How many can you recall in the panic?
practice.hint: Take the blocked facts away from {a}.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}. The blocked facts are not deleted; they come back once you are calm.

practice.prompt: Mia hides how upset she is and acts as if nothing happened. What is this called?
practice.hint: Is she changing the meaning, or pushing the feeling down?
practice.explain: Hiding a feeling is suppression. The feeling stays, and her body stays stressed inside.

practice.prompt: The prefrontal cortex keeps developing until about age 25. Sam is {a}. About how many more years of development are left?
practice.hint: The brake is still being wired until about 25. Subtract Sam’s age, {a}, from 25 to find the years left.
practice.explain: 25 take away {a} is {=25-a} years. The brake keeps getting stronger the whole time.

pool.prompt: What does the prefrontal cortex do when the alarm goes off?
choices: Checks the facts and can calm the alarm
pool.hint: It is the brake, behind your forehead.
pool.explain: The prefrontal cortex checks what is really happening and can calm the amygdala's alarm.

pool.prompt: Why can your mind go blank in a scary exam?
choices: A flood of stress hormones blocks thinking and recall
Your brain deletes what you learned
pool.hint: Remember the stress slider at panic.
pool.explain: High levels of adrenaline and cortisol make the prefrontal cortex work badly. The memories are still there once you calm down.

pool.prompt: Your friend does not reply to your message. Which thought is cognitive reappraisal?
choices: “They might be busy. I'll check later.”
pool.hint: Look for another realistic way to see it.
pool.explain: Reappraisal finds another true-to-life meaning, so the alarm drops. Not caring is suppression.

pool.prompt: Why can thrills and feelings be extra strong at 13?
choices: The reward system is very active while the brake is still developing
pool.hint: Think of the two bars on the age slider.
pool.explain: In the teens the dopamine reward system is very responsive while the prefrontal cortex is still being wired. The brain is developing, not broken.

pool.prompt: What happens inside when you suppress a feeling?
choices: The feeling stays and stress in the body goes up
Your brain stops making stress hormones
pool.hint: Look at the stress meter in the lab.
pool.explain: Research by Gross shows suppressing hides the outside signs, but the feeling stays and heart and stress responses rise.

pool.prompt: Which hormone makes your heart pound within seconds of a fright?
pool.hint: It is the fast fight-or-flight hormone.
pool.explain: Adrenaline acts in seconds. Cortisol builds up over about 20 minutes and keeps you on alert.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a good way to regulate a feeling?
pool.hint: Which one manages the feeling instead of hiding it?
pool.explain: Naming a feeling in words can calm the amygdala. Bottling it up and pretending are suppression.

pool.prompt: Cortisol peaks roughly 20 minutes after a fright. A fright happens {a} minutes into lunch. About how many minutes into lunch does cortisol peak?
pool.hint: Cortisol is the slow stress hormone. Add its 20-minute build-up to the {a} minutes when the fright happened.
pool.explain: {a} + 20 = {=a+20} minutes. Adrenaline acts in seconds, but cortisol builds up slowly and keeps you on alert.

pool.prompt: In a model, alarm level is {a} out of 10. A realistic reappraisal lowers it by {b}. What is the alarm level now?
pool.hint: A realistic new meaning lowers the alarm. Take the drop, {b}, away from the starting level, {a}.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}. Changing the meaning changes the feeling.

pool.prompt: Telling yourself “Everything is perfect!” when it is not. Is that reappraisal?
choices: Yes, if you say it loudly
pool.hint: Reappraisal is another true way to see it.
pool.explain: Reappraisal is not pretending. The new view has to fit the facts, like “I know which topics to practise now.”
